scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users report they cannot reach Server Room or
Internet Lab. router0 and router2 both report RIP routes intact
and can ping each other's interfaces directly. office_pc (on
router1's own LAN) can still ping its gateway 192.168.3.1, but it
too cannot reach the Server Room. What breaks transit through
router1?

injection.action: drop all transit forwarding on router1 (net.ipv4.ip_forward is not writable from the exec context, so use the iptables equivalent: a FORWARD-chain drop)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router1 packet forwarding (FORWARD chain)
Mechanism: A FORWARD-chain DROP rule makes router1 drop every
  packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (transit). Transit
  traffic (it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2 -> pc1) is
  dropped at router1, and office_pc -> Server Room is dropped
  too (it is also transit). Only traffic to router1's OWN
  interfaces still works -- office_pc can still ping its gateway
  192.168.3.1 -- which is the tell that router1 is up but not
  forwarding. RIP keeps running because its sockets are local,
  not forwarded. (This is the iptables equivalent of
  net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, used because that sysctl is not writable
  from the exec context.)
Localization: router1
Root cause: a FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 stops transit
  forwarding (equivalent to ip_forward disabled)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1 (re-enable forwarding)

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** The netfilter FORWARD chain on router1 contains a catch-all DROP rule (`iptables` / `nft` table `ip filter`, chain `FORWARD`): `counter packets 24 bytes 2016 drop` with no match conditions — it matches every forwarded packet regardless of source, destination, protocol, or interface.

**Mechanism:** Linux routes transit packets through the kernel's `FORWARD` netfilter hook before handing them to the outgoing interface. Because the DROP rule has no selectors and sits as the sole explicit rule in the chain (chain policy is ACCEPT, but the explicit rule fires first), every inter-network packet router1 attempts to transit is silently discarded in kernel space. The routers' own interfaces are in the `INPUT` chain, which is untouched, so direct pings **to** router1's own IPs (e.g., office_pc → gateway 192.168.3.1) succeed, giving the false impression that the router is healthy. Router0↔Router2 WAN-link pings also succeed only when directed at directly-connected interface IPs resolved locally — any end-to-end transit still hits FORWARD and is dropped.

**Localization:** router1 only. All four of its interfaces (eth0–eth3 covering lan_office, lan_principle WAN links, and both inter-router WANs) funnel transit through this single FORWARD rule.

**Root cause:** A blanket `DROP` rule was injected into router1's `FORWARD` chain, converting it from a transit router into a firewall that silently discards all inter-network traffic.

**Fix:** Remove the offending rule — `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` — which restores the chain to its default ACCEPT policy and allows RIP-advertised routes to forward traffic normally.

per_axis.rationale: The submission explicitly localizes the fault to router1 and repeatedly describes the DROP rule existing on router1's FORWARD chain.

Correctly recommends deleting the catch-all FORWARD DROP rule (iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP) to restore packet forwarding on router1.
